stories.title: Government jet arrives in Dubai for Kinahan extradition
stories.summary: The new Government jet has arrived in Dubai after departing Ireland this morning, as the operation to extradite Daniel Kinahan back to Ireland continues. The 49-year-old has been detained in Dubai since April, following his arrest under a warrant issued by the Irish courts. He lost his final appeal against his extradition, with Irish authorities now in the process of bringing him back to the country where he is expected to be charged with directing an organised crime group. This morning, the Government's new Dassault Falcon 6X jet left Baldonnell.

stories.title: Call over access to drug to treat Friedreich's Ataxia
stories.summary: Sinn Féin Leader Mary Lou McDonald has called on the Government to ensure families affected by Friedreich's Ataxia can access drugs to treat it. Deputy McDonald said that the drug, Skyclarys, is "scheduled for consideration at a meeting on Tuesday, but the worry is that it will be referred on to yet another committee, another group for another round of consultation and decision". Friedreich's Ataxia is a rare inherited neurological condition that progressively damages the nervous system, affecting mobility, balance, and coordination. Clinical trials suggest Skyclarys - the first and only EU-authorised pharmaceutical treatment for the rare condition - could slow the progression of symptoms. The treatment is already publicly funded in a number of European countries.

stories.title: Taoiseach defends Government jet amid navigation concern
stories.summary: Taoiseach Micheál Martin has reiterated the Coalition's defence of the new Government jet but stopped short of denying reports it may have difficulty landing in fog due to the absence of an Israel-made navigational system. The Journal.ie reported this week how the €53 million aircraft was purchased from a French firm without a FalconEye system, which normally sits on the plane's nose and helps it land in fog or other weather conditions that limit visibility, as it was made by an Israeli manufacturer. The Government adopted a policy in 2024 of not awarding Israeli companies defence contracts owing to an advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice against Israeli settlements in the West Bank. Speaking as he visited Fleadh Cheoil na hÉireann in Belfast, Mr Martin insisted the jet "has been very effective".

stories.title: Supermac's wins UK trademark battle with McDonald's
stories.summary: Supermac's has won the latest round of a long-running legal battle with McDonald’s over trademarks, with the UK Intellectual Property Office ruling that the Irish fast-food chain’s name and logo can be registered in the UK. Supermac’s founder and managing director, Pat McDonagh, said the decision represented another significant legal victory for his company in defending its identity against opposition from the US multinational. McDonald’s unsuccessfully claimed that the registration of Supermac’s marks would conflict with its existing UK trademark rights including "Big Mac" and "McCafé". The ruling is seen as an important development in allowing Supermac’s to move forward on its plans to develop its brand in Britain.

stories.title: Thai teenager kills seven in rampage at home and school
stories.summary: A Thai teenager killed ⁠at least five people and himself at a school outside Bangkok after fatally shooting his grandparents, police said, in the southeast Asian nation's worst mass killing since 2022. Those killed at the school were all teachers and staff and police said the 14-year-old student fired at least 26 bullets using a gun that belonged to his grandfather. An additional 34 rounds were found, police said. Police Colonel Thadsakorn Konthong, superintendent of Bang Bua Thong Police Station, said the boy killed his elderly relatives at around 5am local time (11pm Irish Time yesterday). "The firearm and the bullets belonged to the grandfather," said Thadsakorn. "An initial inspection found signs that the firearm had been searched for inside the grandfather's bedroom."

stories.title: Ward recovers from slow start to claim win over Kasparian
stories.summary: Joe Ward recovered from a slow start to defeat Artjom Kasparian on the undercard of Aaron McKenna's world title fight at the 3Arena in Dublin. Now 32, Ward finally had the opportunity to box on a major show on Irish shores and it certainly delivered in terms of entertainment. Entering what was just a 13th fight in seven years since turning professional, the Moate man described it as the beginning of the last chapter of his career. Defeat would undoubtedly make it a short one. The early signs were not good as he struggled to settle into the contest with Ward out on his feet in the fourth due to sustained pressure from his opponent.

stories.title: St Kilda promise patience as McDonald lands in Melbourne
stories.summary: St Kilda have vowed to be patient with Kobe McDonald after the Mayo hero met up with his new teammates in Melbourne for the first time on Friday to officially begin his Australian adventure. The 18-year-old penned a contract with the Saints last year but stayed in Ireland to finish his Leaving Cert and throw his weight in with the Mayo Gaelic footballers for the championship. Few would have envisioned just how well the summer would go for the brilliant young talent. McDonald was at the heart of his county's glorious run to All-Ireland SFC glory, helping them to a famous win against Kerry in the decider that ended Mayo's 75-year wait for Sam Maguire.

stories.title: Hoops' wild defeat of Dundalk marred by fan confrontation
stories.summary: Shamrock Rovers stretched their lead at the top of the SSE Airtricity Men's Premier Division to 10 points after a wild first half that yielded all five goals and saw a geed-up home fan confront Dundalk players on the pitch. By full-time, referee Rob Harvey had dished out 11 yellow cards - including to both managers - having also shown Rovers coach Sean Kavanagh a red in the tunnel at half-time. It was an all-or-nothing sort of night in Tallaght, and you couldn't take your eyes off it. Dundalk were the only team Rovers hadn’t beaten this season but the Hoops’ first-half display was littered with so many mistakes, it’s a wonder how they led on three occasions through Dylan Watts, Michael Noonan and Jonathan Afolabi.

stories.title: Get Creative: The art of hospitality – self-portrait as a host 2
stories.summary: In a new series, acclaimed artist Jennie Moran explores the road to developing a successful art practice. Jennie is a visual artist whose work explores hospitality as a creative and connective philosophy. stories.title: Armagh Observatory to host special event for solar eclipse
stories.summary: On Wednesday, 12 August, the moon will cover approximately 94% of the sun, causing a partial solar eclipse. It will be the deepest eclipse seen from the UK and Ireland since the total eclipse of August 1999, and the last time that such an eclipse will be seen here until 2090. A total solar eclipse will cover a narrow path of our planet, likely crossing Greenland, Iceland, northern Spain, and a small portion of Portugal. Although Ireland won't see a total eclipse, the 94% partial eclipse has been eagerly awaited by professionals in the field for decades.

stories.summary: Aaron McKenna claimed the vacant IBF world middleweight title after beating Etinosa Oliha by unanimous decision as a lifelong dream came true in his first bout on Irish soil at the 3Arena in Dublin. The Monaghan man, who trains alongside his brother Stevie under father Fergal, thrilled a passionate and noisy support base that made the trip to the capital for a long-awaited homecoming and chance at world honours. Italian fighter Oliha had claimed an IBO world title previously as part of a perfect record in 22 fights, two more than McKenna, but had not fought outside of his home country or Germany. McKenna was to finally hear the roar of his people after long spells in England, the US and even further afield.

stories.title: Government insists new jet can land in bad weather
stories.summary: The Coalition has insisted there are no issues with a new Government jet after reports it may struggle to land in bad weather. It has been suggested the new aircraft may not be able to land in foggy weather as it was ordered without key navigation equipment from an Israeli firm. The Government adopted a policy in 2024 of not awarding Israeli companies defence contracts owing to an advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice against Israeli settlements in the West Bank. The Journal.ie reported how the €53 million aircraft was purchased from a French firm without a FalconEye system, which normally sits on the plane's nose and helps it land in fog or other weather conditions that limit visibility, as it was made by an Israeli manufacturer.

stories.title: Kingspan raises profit forecast on data centre demand
stories.summary: Shares in insulation and building materials group Kingspan jumped almost 20% in Dublin trade today after it raised its full-year profit guidance. Kingspan said it was raising its guidance due to its data centre construction operations that it says are benefiting from a burgeoning tech sector which is detached from the regular economy. Co Cavan-based Kingspan expects full-year trading profit to jump by about 18% to €1.13 billion, up from a forecast of €1.05 billion in late April. The company said it can also reasonably expect to break through €10 billion in annual revenue for the first time.

stories.title: The extraordinary life and times of Kerry music mogul Bill Fuller
stories.summary: Analysis: A new film tells the little-known story of the pioneering venue owner and colourful music promoter whose business empire spanned the globe Here's a question to consider - and it says a lot about national values. When Irish people go out for the night: (i) should they dance domestic dances under the close supervision of priests and holy men or (ii) should they be allowed to dance to well-known local and international names in venues operated as businesses? If you chose option (ii) you might have Bill Fuller to thank. And, like most Irish people, you’ve probably never heard his name. When Ireland achieved independence, politicians turned their attention to what it meant to be Irish. How could Ireland keep its traditional values in a rapidly changing world? A large part of this national public discussion focused on the threat from abroad. The Catholic hierarchy wanted to safeguard the country from anything that could undermine the moral order. The Church was very worried about communism, 'immoral’ films and rock ‘n’ roll. But one of the biggest challenges to the Catholic hierarchy didn't come from Moscow or Memphis but from the mountains of Co Kerry. When the Catholic hierarchy and members of the Irish judiciary were preaching against the 'evils' of jazz music, Fuller was bringing prominent jazz musicians and rock 'n’ roll acts, including Stan Kenton, to perform in Ireland.

stories.title: Iran issues demands for reopening of Strait of Hormuz
stories.summary: Iran set preconditions for a reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, including compensation for war damages, complicating a potential deal to open the waterway essential to the world economy. Tehran has imposed an effective blockade of the strait since the United States and Israel struck Iran in late February, and wants to charge tolls for passage, attacking ships it accuses of attempting to circumvent its preferred route. Continued attacks in the strait, which was free to transit before the war, led to the collapse of an April ceasefire. Mediators have since urged both sides to return to the terms of a June memorandum.

stories.title: Kilkee residents vow to continue wastewater plant fight
stories.summary: Residents of Kilkee, Co Clare, say they will continue to fight plans by Uisce Éireann to build a wastewater treatment plant in the coastal resort. Over 150 people attended a public meeting in Kilkee, following the failure of a High Court challenge against the development earlier this summer. Campaigners said they may have lost this judicial review but the challenge is not over and that they have now applied to the High Court, seeking leave to appeal its ruling directly to the Supreme Court. The Kilkee cliff walk is a huge summer attraction in the town. Now, local residents say plans by Uisce Éireann to push ahead with a sewage treatment plant on a nearby site is "devastating".

stories.title: Unexpected job losses in US last month
stories.summary: The US economy unexpectedly shed jobs in July and nonfarm payrolls for the previous month were revised sharply lower, potentially raising questions about whether the Federal Reserve will increase interest rates next month. Nonfarm payrolls decreased by 23,000 jobs last month after a downwardly revised 20,000 increase in June, the Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics said in its closely watched employment report today. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast payrolls rising 80,000 after advancing by a previously reported 57,000 in June. Estimates ranged from as low as 10,000 to as high as 140,000 jobs added. Payrolls, however, have a tendency to be softer in July. Economists have viewed the labour market as being in a "slow hire, slow fire" mode.

stories.title: Camogie team news: Galway trio are passed fit
stories.summary: Galway are set to stick with their tried and tested method for Sunday's All-Ireland senior camogie final against Cork after manager Cathal Murray made no changes from the team that defeated Kilkenny in the semis. There were a number of injury concerns for the defending champions, after Aoife Donohue and Dervla Higgins came off injured against the Cats, and Carrie Dolan finished the game moving gingerly. But all three are included as the Connacht side aim to defend an All-Ireland title at senior level for the first time. Niamh Mallon, who has been unavailable in recent weeks, is named on the bench. Cork, who are going for their third title in four seasons, have also named an unchanged side from the one that saw off Tipperary the last day.
